replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper6578 by Reviewer 2dys

content.title: Response to reviewer 2dys
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback! We highly value each of your comments, and all your concerns are addressed point by point:
***
**Concern1. The current writing makes the paper a bit hard to follow as notations and algorithms are all in the appendix. Also, some notations are missing such as n, \mathcal{M}. I recommend the authors to explain the notations early in the method section and clarify the benefits when using algorithms 2 to 3 and then to algorithm 1. The main text should be self-contained per se.**

Sorry for the inconvenience caused by the writing. We have been working on improving the readability of our paper and uploading a revised version with highlights.  Specifically, in response to your suggestions: 
* We moved the notations from the appendix into the main text of our paper, as shown in Table 1. 
*  We streamlined the number of notations listed in the notation table as much as possible to avoid confusing readers with too many notations and definitions. For those notations not listed in the notation table, we provided a corresponding explanation at where the notations are used for the first time. For example, $n$ is the batch size, and $\mathcal{M}$ is the current pruning mask. 
* We clarify the benefits of using different algorithms at the end of their corresponding subsections in section METHODOLOGY. For example, we highlighted the benefit of using Unified Pruning over Simple Pruning (renamed as "Multimodal Pruning" in the revised paper) "Unified search on different modalities further enables Unified Pruning to automatically assign appropriate pruning ratios to all compressible components." and the benefit of using UPop over Unified Pruning is "Progressive Pruning eliminates the gap of parameter weights between the searched model and the pruned subnet to be retrained, therefore gaining better convergence and performance." 
*  We reorganized the storyline of Section METHODOLOGY and made the main text self-contained. 
* We provided more explanations in the section METHODOLOGY to help readers better understand our approach. 

For your convenience of comparison, we have highlighted the main modifications. We would appreciate it if you could take a moment to check out our revised paper.

***

**Concern2. Why the paper limits itself to pruning only? Parameters sharing is also an effective approach for model compression and it can be done in a similar manner using learnable masks in [0,1].**

The pruning paradigm proposed by UPop can also be further adapted to Parameters Sharing. And the reason why we currently choose Pruning to implement our paradigm concretely is that, to our knowledge, Pruning enables the reduction of parameters and FLOPs simultaneously, while Parameter Sharing typically only reduces the number of parameters. The proposed UPop is orthogonal to Parameters Sharing, which can be combined without conflicts for a larger compression ratio.
***
**Concern3. It is a bit unclear to me why the authors used the term “heterogeneous structures”. Please clarify a bit more on this. How do you ensure the normalized masks in Eq. 4 belong to the same distribution? And why is this necessary?**

* Heterogeneous refers to compressible components with different mechanisms of computation, while homogeneous refers to compressible components with the same mechanisms of computation. For example, Self-Attention and MLP are heterogeneous structures, while Self-Attention and Cross-Attention are homogeneous structures. To avoid possible confusing words as much as possible, the revised paper uses the word "different" to replace the word "heterogeneous."
* Thank you for pointing out this issue. By normalization, the distribution of different masks is close in magnitude and therefore becomes comparable, which boosts the compression performance effectively. We have accordingly adjusted the description to "transforming the magnitudes distributions of different structures' masks to have the same mean and standard deviation, and thus masks used for different structures can be comparable," The highlighted modification can be found at the middle of page 5 in our revised paper.
* This transformation is necessary because the magnitude of the learned masks used for different structures varies greatly. Without the transformation, the magnitude of the learned masks is incomparable, resulting in Unified Search being biased towards certain structures.
***
We hope that our response has adequately addressed your concerns. Please do not hesitate to let us know if you have new comments on our work or you need further clarifications that we can provide.

content.title: Response to reviewer vBgg
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback! We highly value each of your comments, and all your concerns are addressed point by point:
***
**Concern1. This paper only compares to simple pruning and unified pruning. More strong baselines are needed.**

To our knowledge, UPop is the first work on multimodal Transformer pruning. Therefore it is difficult to find stronger baselines that can be used for a fair comparison. Actually, the approach we denoted as "Simple Pruning" is straightforwardly applying the SOTA unimodal pruning approach, ViT-Slimming, to the multimodal scenario, and this SOTA unimodal pruning is a strong baseline in unimodal tasks. 

To compare with the SOTA pruning approach, which only applies to unimodal tasks,  we also adapt UPop to the unimodal task and model on unimodal tasks. Experimental results of compressing DeiT on ImageNet are reported in Table 12 and Figure 4 in the Appendix of the revised paper we just submitted.  UPop can also achieve competitive performance compared to other unimodal compression SOTA approaches. For example, UPop achieves a 2$\times$ compression ratio with a mere 1.0% accuracy drop, and a 30% compression ratio with an even 0.3% accuracy boost. 
|  Approach   | Top-1 Acc | Top-5 Acc | Params | FLOPs
|  ----  | ----  | ----  | ----  | ----  | 
| DeiT[1]  | 79.9 | 95.0 | 22.0 | 4.6 |
| GLiT[2] | 80.5 | - | 24.6 | 4.4 |
| DynamicViT[3] | 79.3 | - | 22.0 | 2.9 |
| S$^2$ViTE[4] | 79.2 | - | 14.6 | 3.1|
| ViTAS[5] | 80.2 | 95.1 | 23.0 |  4.9 |
| ViT-Slimming[6] | 77.9 | 94.1 | 11.4 | 2.3 |
| EViT[7] | 78.5 | 94.2  | 22.0 | 2.3|
| A-ViT[8] | 78.6 | - | 22.0 |  3.6 |
| **UPop 1.11x** | 81.1 | 95.4 | 19.9 | 4.1 |
| **UPop 1.25x** | 80.8 | 95.4 | 17.8 | 3.7 |
| **UPop 1.42x** | 80.2 | 95.1 | 15.7 | 3.2 |
| **UPop 1.67x** | 79.6 | 94.8 | 13.5 | 2.8 |
| **UPop 2x** | 78.9 | 94.6 | 11.4 | 2.3 |

For more detailed experimental results, e.g., the Accuracy-FLOPs trade-off comparison chart and the Accuracy-Parameter trade-off comparison chart, we would appreciate it if you could take a moment to check out Appendix B.5 of our revised paper.

***
**Concern2. The proposed method seems not for multimodal-specific tasks. Evaluations on more modalities, including single modality, are needed.**

Although our work mainly focused on the compression of multimodal tasks, it can also be adapted to the single modality by stripping Unified Search on different modalities. We have added corresponding experiments as stated in the answer to the Concern1.

***
We hope that our response has adequately addressed your concerns. Please do not hesitate to let us know if you have new comments on our work or you need further clarifications that we can provide.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3JnZ
content.comment:
Thanks for your feedback! We highly value each of your comments, and all your concerns are addressed point by point:
***
**Concern1. The text is hard to follow, the notations are given in the appendix, there isn't a single figure to illustrate the method.**

Sorry for the inconvenience caused by the writing. We have been working on improving the readability of our paper and uploading a revised version with highlights. We reconstructed the writing of the paper, especially for the Section METHODOLOGY. Specifically, in response to your suggestions:
* We moved the notations from the appendix into the main text of our paper, as shown in Table 1, and then we reduced the number of notations to mitigate the problem of reading confusion. 
*  We added Figure 1 to illustrate the pipeline of our approach. 
*  To give readers a more comprehensive understanding of our approach, we combined "Unified Pruning" and "Progressive Pruning" into a single subsection, "Unified and Progressive Pruning." 
*  We provided more explanations in the section METHODOLOGY to help readers better understand our approach. 

For your convenience of comparison, we have highlighted the main modifications. We would appreciate it if you could take a moment to check out our revised paper.

***

**Concern2. The method is specifically designed to ViTs and thus seem a bit limited.**

UPop is a multimodal compression approach that can be used for any multimodal model. For example, we provide experiments on mix-stream multimodal architecture, BLIP,  as shown in Table 1;  experiments on dual-stream multimodal architecture, CLIP, as shown in Table 6. The proposed UPop can also be applied on unimodal compression, as shown in Table 12. We mainly consider Transformer-based architecture, while the compression technique can be easily extended to Convolution-based architecture by adapting the shape of the trainable masks only.

***

**Concern3.  The paper technical novelty is limited as it provides an incremented improvement over [1]**

Compared with [1], our proposed UPop is different  in 3 aspects:
* Unified Pruning enables adaptively instead of manually assigning the appropriate pruning ratio to each compressible component, and Progressive Pruning gains better convergence and performance at high compression ratios. However, [1] manually assigns each compressible component with a compression ratio, which is inefficient and sub-optimal. Moreover, the paradigm retraining after the search used by [1] fails when it comes to higher compression ratios.
* The subnets searched by UPop support real deployment without specific hardware requirements. However, [1] cannot do it since 
heads pruned by [1] within a layer have different dimensions, and thus matrix computation of the attention map becomes unfeasible on regular devices. 
* UPop focuses on the compression of vision-language tasks and can also be applied to unimodal tasks, like image classification. However, [1] is only applied  for unimodal tasks.

These differences are also highlighted at the end of the section Related Work. 
***
We hope that our response has adequately addressed your concerns. Please do not hesitate to let us know if you have new comments on our work or you need further clarifications that we can provide.

content.title: General Response and Summary of Updates in Our Revised Submission
content.comment:
We sincerely thank all reviewers for their time and constructive suggestions on our work, which have helped us improve our work a lot. Our work has received encouragement and recognition from reviewers. Reviewer vBgg finds our approach "interesting and intuitive," and our experimental results are "promising"; reviewer 2dys also agrees that our work is "novel," our experiments are "done carefully," and our analysis is "useful and convincing." We first briefly summarize the main updates in our revised paper in this post and then respond to each reviewer through individual posts.
***
We have updated our submission to include changes according to reviewers' suggestions as follows:
* To improve the readability of our work and make the main text self-contained, we reconstructed the writing of the paper, especially for Section METHODOLOGY. 
* We moved notation tables from the Appendix to the main text, as shown in Table 1, and streamlined the number of necessary notations. 
* We added a new diagram to illustrate our proposed UPop, as shown in Figure 1. 
* We adapted UPop to the unimodal task and model, and compared UPop with more strong baselines, as shown in Table 12 and Figure 4.
* We added new charts to report detailed training hyperparameters and structure hyperparameters used in all our experiments, as shown in Table 7, Table 8, and Table 9.

We highlighted the main modifications of the revised submission in blue, and we would appreciate it if you could take a moment to check out our revised submission.
***
Moreover, in recent days we have also been working on validating the effectiveness of UPop on more tasks, datasets, and model architectures. We update our submission including newly added experiments as follows: 
* Compress BLIP-VQA on the Visual Question Answering task (Table 4) 
* Compress BLIP-Retrieval on the Flickr30K dataset of the Image-Text Retrieval task (Table 5) 
* Compress CLIP on the COCO dataset and Flickr30K dataset of the Image-Text Retrieval task (Table 6) 

UPop has also achieved very competitive performance on these newly added experiments. The experiments that UPop has completed so far can be summarized as

| Task  | Model  | Dataset | Compression Ratios | Chapter | 
| :------ | :------ | :------ | :------ | :------ |
|  Visual Reasoning | BLIP-NLVR | NVLR2 |  2x,3x,4x,5x,10x | Section 4.1 | 
|  Image Captioning | BLIP-Caption | COCO | 2x,4x | Section 4.5 | 
| Visual Question Answer | BLIP-VQA | VQAv2 | 2x,4x | Section 4.6 | 
| Image-Text Retrieval |  BLIP-Retrieval | COCO | 2x,4x | Section 4.7 | 
| Image-Text Retrieval |  BLIP-Retrieval | Flickr30K | 2x,4x | Section 4.7 | 
| Image-Text Retrieval |  CLIP | COCO | 2x,4x | Section 4.7 | 
| Image-Text Retrieval |  CLIP | Flickr30K | 2x,4x | Section 4.7 | 
| Image Classification | DeiT | ImageNet | 1.11x, 1.25x, 1.42x, 1.67x, 2x | Appendix B.5 |

***
If there are further clarifications that we can provide or you have new comments on our work, please do not hesitate to let us know.

content.title: Contributions to the Community
content.comment:
Dear reviewers and AC,

Many thanks for your valuable time. After improving our work based on your constructive suggestions and clarifying all of the concerns that reviewers have raised, we would also like to share the contribution of our work to the community briefly.

This is **the first work to investigate multimodal Transformer pruning**, whose effectiveness is **systematically validated on a broad range** of tasks (e.g., Visual Reasoning, Image Captioning, Visual Question Answer, Image-Text Retrieval, Text-Image Retrieval, and Image Classification), datasets (e.g., NLVR2, COCO, VQAv2, Flickr30K, and ImageNet), and model architectures (e.g., CLIP, BLIPs, and DeiT). In addition to the first multimodal Transformer pruning approach itself, which will **inspire further explorations in this emerging field**, this work also provides compressed performance on various tasks, datasets, model architectures, and compression ratios, which can be served as **comprehensive baselines for a lot of future works**.

We believe all our reviewers and AC have a high level of academic insight, and will stand at a higher angle to judge a paper also based on its broader contribution to our community. Publishing this work has no harm to ICLR and can draw more attention from our community to this emerging field and further advance the field of multimodal compression.

Best wishes,

Paper6578 Authors
